title: Germline EGFR T790M mutation and lung cancer risk.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Europe PMC record (open-access flags all 'N', no PMCID, hasSuppl=N, no text-mined accessions, no NCBI GEO/SRA/BioProject/dbGaP links); Zenodo API search (31 unrelated EGFR hits, none this study); Dryad API search (0 results); GWAS Catalog REST lookup for PMID 42752144 (endpoint returned HTTP 410); Science article page and two supplementary-file URLs (all HTTP 403, paywalled); 23andMe's public data-access policy pages.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the study design and numbers: >3.3 million 23andMe research participants, 641 T790M carriers out of >10 million consented, carrier frequency ~1 in 15,850, ~25-fold lung cancer risk overall and >60-fold in never-smokers, no excess risk for 17 other cancers, Southern Appalachian founder event ~200-225 years ago. These come from the abstract, the Dana-Farber press release and the ASCO Post summary, not from any file I opened.

a1_downloadable.note: FAIL, and this is fatal. The study is built on 23andMe's proprietary research cohort. 23andMe releases only de-identified GWAS (genome-wide association study) summary statistics, and only after a Statement of Work plus Data Transfer Agreement signed by both institutions, capped at 10,000 SNPs (single-nucleotide polymorphisms) for meta-analysis. No individual-level genotype or phenotype data is obtainable. No deposit exists in Zenodo, Dryad, GWAS Catalog, or any NCBI archive. The paper itself is paywalled (HTTP 403) and has no PubMed Central copy, so even the supplementary tables could not be opened. The two replication cohorts named in press coverage, UK Biobank and All of Us, are themselves controlled access requiring applications.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Not assessed; stopped at A1. The label (lung cancer diagnosis) is a self-reported survey field inside 23andMe's private database, so it cannot be inspected.

a3_inputs_present.note: Not assessed; stopped at A1. Genotypes are individual-level human data that 23andMe never releases.

a5_enough_rows.note: Not assessed; stopped at A1. Note separately that the informative unit is the carrier, and press coverage reports 641 carriers in 23andMe, 2 in UK Biobank and 19 in All of Us, so even with access the variant-carrier sample would be far under the ~1,500-row bar.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Not assessed; stopped at A1. No file exists against which to check the 3.3 million or 641 figures.

a8_label_provenance.note: Not assessed; stopped at A1. The outcome is self-reported lung cancer from consumer survey responses, which would need scrutiny if the data were ever obtainable.

honest_claim_h3: No claim is possible: the underlying data is a private consumer-genetics cohort that cannot be downloaded, so no model can be trained or checked.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a person's inherited DNA and smoking history to predict whether they will develop lung cancer.
plain_idea.train_on: The project considered would use each participant's genotype (in particular whether they carry the EGFR T790M variant, a single inherited DNA letter change), their smoking status, ancestry and a polygenic risk score. The paper reports more than 3.3 million participants, but I could not verify any count in a file.
plain_idea.predict: Whether the person is ever diagnosed with lung cancer. The true answer comes from self-reported cancer diagnoses collected through 23andMe's participant surveys.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Clinicians deciding who should get computed-tomography lung screening currently use smoking history alone; a model that flags high-risk never-smokers would change screening eligibility. But the question is already answered by the paper's own odds ratios, and the data to build such a model is not public.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: predict lung cancer onset from germline genotype plus smoking status in a very large consumer-genetics cohort, with the rare EGFR T790M variant as the headline feature. Dead on access, and dead a second time on sample size, since only 641 variant carriers exist in the whole 23andMe cohort and 2 and 19 respectively in UK Biobank and All of Us.

effort.compute_note: Not estimated; no data can be obtained, so there is nothing to size.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Look for a data availability deposit under the DOI. I checked Europe PMC, Zenodo, Dryad, GWAS Catalog and NCBI in one pass and found none; 23andMe's own policy page then confirms that only 10,000-SNP summary statistics are shareable, and only under a signed institutional agreement. Five minutes of work kills it.

verdict_reason: Part A1 failure: the data is 23andMe's private cohort, released only as capped summary statistics under a signed institutional Data Transfer Agreement, with nothing deposited in any public repository and the paper itself paywalled. Even with access, the informative unit is the variant carrier, and there are only 641 of them across 3.3 million people, well below any usable training-set size. This is a classic epidemiological association study, not a modellable table.
